hero.headline: Three years. Three approaches. One dataset.
hero.subhead: How HAVC's published PDFs became a structured, auditable, navigable registry — what worked at each step, what broke, and what it cost.

eras.label: Era 1
eras.title: Custom GPT with all the PDFs in the knowledge base

system.input: ≈ 1,100 PDFs uploaded to a custom GPT
process: retrieval over the PDF knowledge base

eras.what: I uploaded HAVC's published PDFs into a custom GPT's knowledge base and started asking it questions. Zero engineering effort. Immediate utility for one-off questions.
why_good: Useful as a fuzzy search engine.
Cost: minutes of setup. No code. No infrastructure.
Good first answer to 'can I just throw the PDFs at an LLM and get something useful?' — yes, you can.
why_limited: Retrieval-only — it could find a relevant PDF, but couldn't aggregate across them.
Numbers hallucinated freely. There was no way to ask it for 'total funded in 2018' and trust the answer.
No audit trail. No way to ask 'how do you know'.
No API. Only a chat box.

artifacts.text: No local artifacts — the GPT lived in OpenAI's platform. What remains is the lesson: retrieval over PDFs does not produce a dataset, only a slightly better way to ask a search engine.

eras.label: Era 2
eras.title: Constrained extraction in two Python scripts

system.output: master_financing.csv · 2.1 MB · rows of (title, amount, year)

eras.what: Wrote two Python scripts. One opened each PDF, looked for funding tables, and pulled rows into a CSV. The other merged the per-PDF output by programme (natječaj). The whole corpus ran in under an hour with no LLM cost.
why_good: Structured. Reproducible. Auditable line by line.
Cheap: deterministic parsing, no per-document API calls.

Successfully extracted the table-shaped majority of funding decisions — only ten files in the whole corpus had no rows at all, and they turned out to be administrative documents (job postings, regulations, the HAVC statute), not funding decisions.
why_limited: Only the tables. The jury rationale text — why a project was funded, what the panel said — was discarded.
No project identity. The same film appearing across script-development, production, and distribution rounds showed up as three unrelated rows.
No people. Producer, director, writer fields were inconsistent or blank.
Numbers were locked in without verification. Comma-vs-period decimals, OCR drift, and 'HRK vs EUR' got silently wrong on a long tail of rows.
No way to ask the data anything beyond 'sum this column'.

artifacts.note: The first extractor — table-only, deterministic, no LLM

eras.label: Era 3
eras.title: Pipeline, classifier, agentic audit loops

system.output: dataset/master.json · 14 MB · 989 records · 10,388 rows · with narratives, people, project identity

eras.what: Replaced the single-script approach with a modular pipeline. Each PDF is first classified by document type, then routed to the right extractor — tables, jury narratives, OCR'd scans. Project identity is resolved by normalising titles across documents. Amounts run through a dedicated parser. Then the output runs through audit passes that produce machine-readable reports of every gap and every suspicious value. Claude and Codex sessions iterate on those reports: patching prompts, refining the amount parser, backfilling missing fields, and dropping rows that turn out to be artefacts.
why_good: Every record is auditable: original PDF, page number, raw text, normalised value.
Every gap has a written report (_amount_repair, _bogus_rows_drop, _backfill, _narratives_backfill).
The pipeline is restartable — cached extractions get reused.
Captures the parts Era 2 dropped: jury narratives, people, project identity across rounds, session totals.
Numbers are challenged. The amount-repair pass alone inspected 116 suspect rows and confirmed or fixed 37 of them.
why_limited: Some amounts still drift on edge cases — the dashboard surfaces those for human review (80 rows remain flagged 'needs_review' even after Pass B).
Heavy in compute and tokens. 226 Claude sessions and a similar count of Codex turns in 48 hours.
The pipeline assumes HAVC's PDF conventions hold. New layouts will need new classifier rules.
